description: Atomic models, alpha, beta and gamma radiation, half-life calculations and nuclear equations.
content_html:
How Our Understanding of the Atom Developed

The model of the atom has changed several times as new evidence became available — a classic example of how scientific explanations develop with evidence (IaS3). Early in the 19th century, John Dalton proposed that matter is made of tiny, indivisible solid spheres. This explained chemical reactions but had no internal structure.

In the late 19th century, J.J. Thomson discovered the electron and replaced Dalton's model with the plum pudding model — a positive sphere with electrons dotted through it like plums in a pudding. This was overturned in 1910–1911 when Rutherford, Geiger and Marsden fired alpha particles at thin gold foil. Most particles passed straight through, but some deflected sharply and a small fraction bounced back. The only explanation was a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus surrounded by mostly empty space.

Key Fact

The Rutherford-Geiger-Marsden alpha particle scattering experiment (published 1911) provided evidence for the nuclear model. Bohr later refined this by proposing electrons occupy fixed energy levels (shells) around the nucleus. James Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932, completing the modern picture.

Atomic Structure

Every atom has a nucleus containing protons and neutrons, surrounded by electrons in energy levels. Atoms are extremely small — on the order of \(10^{-10}\) m across — and the nucleus is about a hundred-thousandth of the diameter of the whole atom.

An element is defined by its number of protons (atomic number). Different forms of the same element that have different numbers of neutrons are called isotopes. We write isotopes in nuclear notation as \(^A_Z X\), where \(A\) is the mass number (protons + neutrons) and \(Z\) is the atomic number (protons).

Types of Radioactive Decay

Some atomic nuclei are unstable and emit radiation to become more stable — they are radioactive. Radioactive decay is a random process: you cannot predict when any particular nucleus will decay. There are four types of emission:

Alpha (\(\alpha\)) — two protons and two neutrons (a helium-4 nucleus: \(^4_2\text{He}\)). Strongly ionising; stopped by a few centimetres of air or a sheet of paper. In decay, mass number decreases by 4 and atomic number decreases by 2.

Beta (\(\beta\)) — a high-speed electron emitted when a neutron in the nucleus converts to a proton. Moderately ionising; stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium. Atomic number increases by 1; mass number unchanged.

Gamma (\(\gamma\)) — high-frequency electromagnetic radiation emitted from the nucleus after other decay. Weakly ionising; only significantly reduced by several centimetres of lead or metres of concrete. No change in mass number or atomic number.

Neutron emission — occasionally an unstable nucleus emits a neutron. Mass number decreases by 1; atomic number unchanged.

Example nuclear equation for alpha decay of radium-226: \(^{226}_{88}\text{Ra} \rightarrow ^{222}_{86}\text{Rn} + ^4_2\text{He}\). Check: top numbers balance (226 = 222 + 4) ✓; bottom numbers balance (88 = 86 + 2) ✓.

Key Fact

Ionising power and penetrating power are inversely related: alpha is most ionising, least penetrating (stopped by paper); gamma is least ionising, most penetrating (requires lead or thick concrete to reduce significantly).

Half-Life

As a radioactive sample decays, the number of unstable nuclei decreases over time, so the activity (number of decays per second) also decreases. The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time it takes for either the number of undecayed nuclei, or the activity (measured in becquerels, Bq), to halve.

After one half-life: half the original nuclei remain. After two half-lives: a quarter remain. After three half-lives: one eighth remain. This pattern can be used to read off half-life from an activity-time graph, or to calculate the fraction remaining after a given number of half-lives.

A radioactive sample has an initial activity of 3200 Bq. After 60 days the activity is 200 Bq. Calculate the half-life.

Count the halvings: 3200 → 1600 → 800 → 400 → 200. That is 4 halvings.

4 half-lives = 60 days, so one half-life = \(\frac{60}{4} = 15\) days.

You can also calculate from an activity-time graph by reading off the time it takes for activity to halve at any point on the decay curve — the half-life is the same throughout (a property of exponential decay).

Contamination and Irradiation

Contamination means radioactive material has been deposited on or inside the body (e.g. ingested or inhaled). This is particularly dangerous because the source continues to irradiate nearby cells indefinitely until it decays or is removed. Irradiation is exposure to an external radiation source — once the source is removed, exposure stops. Alpha particles are especially dangerous if a source is inside the body (high ionising power), but outside the body they are stopped by skin and pose less risk.
exam_tip_html: For nuclear equations, always check that both the mass numbers (top) and atomic numbers (bottom) balance on each side — this is a quick way to find a missing particle. For half-life calculations, use the step-halving method (3200 → 1600 → 800 ...) to count half-lives rather than trying to use logarithms at GCSE. On activity-time graphs, the half-life can be read at any point — it should be the same wherever you measure it. A common error is confusing contamination (source inside the body — ongoing risk) with irradiation (external source — risk stops when source moves away). Questions on the development of the atomic model require you to name the scientists (Dalton, Thomson, Rutherford/Geiger/Marsden, Bohr, Chadwick) and state what evidence or discovery led to each model revision.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The atomic model developed from Dalton's solid sphere → Thomson's plum pudding → Rutherford's nuclear model (from alpha scattering, published 1911) → Bohr's energy levels. Chadwick discovered the neutron in 1932. Each change was driven by new experimental evidence.
  • Alpha (\(^4_2\text{He}\)), beta (electron), gamma (EM wave) and neutron emissions differ in ionising power, penetrating power and effect on the nucleus. Nuclear equations must balance mass number and atomic number on both sides.
  • Half-life is the time for activity to halve. After \(n\) half-lives, the fraction remaining is \(\left(\frac{1}{2}\right)^n\). Contamination (source inside body) is more dangerous than irradiation (external source) because exposure continues after the source moves away.

practice_questions.text: State two differences between alpha particles and gamma rays.
practice_questions.marks:
Any two differences, 1 mark each:
- Alpha particles consist of two protons and two neutrons (helium nuclei); gamma rays are high-frequency electromagnetic waves (no mass or charge).
- Alpha particles are stopped by paper / a few cm of air; gamma rays require several cm of lead or metres of concrete.
- Alpha particles are strongly ionising; gamma rays are weakly ionising.
- Alpha emission reduces mass number by 4 and atomic number by 2; gamma emission does not change mass number or atomic number.

practice_questions.text: A radioactive isotope has an activity of 6400 Bq. After 80 minutes, its activity has fallen to 400 Bq. Calculate the half-life.
practice_questions.marks:
Count halvings: 6400 → 3200 → 1600 → 800 → 400 = 4 half-lives [1 mark]
4 half-lives = 80 minutes → half-life = \(80 / 4 = 20\) minutes [1 mark]

Common error: dividing 80 by 6400 rather than counting the halvings.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the plum pudding model of the atom was replaced by the nuclear model. Refer to the experimental evidence in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: states an experiment was done with gold foil.
Secure: the Rutherford-Geiger-Marsden experiment fired alpha particles at thin gold foil; most passed straight through (consistent with mostly empty space), but some were deflected and a few bounced straight back — this was not predicted by the plum pudding model (which assumed a diffuse positive charge and would allow all particles through with only small deflections).
Mastering: as Secure, plus explains that bouncing back required a tiny, very dense, positively charged region (nucleus) repelling the positive alpha particles — the nuclear model was proposed to fit this evidence; the model was accepted because it explained all the observations.

[1 mark: experiment correctly described (alpha particles, gold foil); 1 mark: key result described (most pass through, some deflect, few bounce back); 1 mark: explains why the plum pudding model could not account for the results and what the nuclear model proposed]

practice_questions.text:
Balance the following nuclear equation for the alpha decay of polonium-210:
\(^{210}_{84}\text{Po} \rightarrow ^{A}_{Z}\text{Pb} + ^{4}_{2}\text{He}\)
State the values of A and Z.
practice_questions.marks:
A = 210 − 4 = 206 [1 mark]
Z = 84 − 2 = 82 [1 mark]

So the daughter nucleus is \(^{206}_{82}\text{Pb}\) (lead-206).

Verification: 210 = 206 + 4 ✓; 84 = 82 + 2 ✓.

practice_questions.text: Explain the difference between contamination by a radioactive material and irradiation by a radioactive source. In your answer, discuss how the half-life of a material affects the hazard it presents.
practice_questions.marks:
Developing: distinguishes contamination (source inside body) from irradiation (external source).
Secure:
- Contamination: radioactive material deposited on or inside the body; source continues to irradiate nearby tissue even if the external source is moved away — ongoing risk.
- Irradiation: exposure to radiation from an external source; risk ceases when the source is removed.
- Half-life significance: a long half-life means slow decay, so the material remains hazardous for a long time; a very short half-life decays quickly but initially high activity poses an acute risk; in contamination, short half-life may be preferable in medical contexts (e.g. tracers) as activity decreases quickly inside the body.
Mastering: as Secure, plus discusses which radiation type is most dangerous in each context (alpha is strongly ionising inside the body — dangerous in contamination; less hazardous as irradiation because it is stopped by skin); links this to IaS4 risk-benefit analysis when making decisions about using radioactive materials in medicine.

[1 mark: contamination correctly defined; 1 mark: irradiation correctly defined and contrasted; 1 mark: explains why contamination is more hazardous; 1 mark: half-life linked to duration of hazard; 1 mark: named radiation type linked to contamination vs irradiation hazard]

practice_questions.text: A patient is given a radioactive tracer for a medical scan. The tracer has a half-life of 6 hours and an initial activity of 800 Bq. Calculate the activity after 24 hours, and explain why a short half-life is preferred for medical tracers.
practice_questions.marks:
Calculation [3 marks]:
24 hours = 4 half-lives (24 ÷ 6 = 4) [1 mark]
Fraction remaining = \((\frac{1}{2})^4 = \frac{1}{16}\) [1 mark]
Activity = \(800 \times \frac{1}{16} = 50\) Bq [1 mark]

Explanation [3 marks]:
Emerging: states a short half-life is safer.
Secure: short half-life means the tracer decays rapidly, so the patient is only exposed to significant radiation for a short time; the activity falls to safe levels quickly, reducing the total radiation dose to the patient.
Mastering: as Secure, plus notes the trade-off — the half-life must be long enough for imaging to be completed before the activity falls too low (risk-benefit: IaS4); also acknowledges that gamma-emitting tracers are used because gamma rays pass out of the body for detection, while alpha emitters inside the body would cause greater cell damage due to high ionising power.

[1 mark: correct calculation of 4 half-lives; 1 mark: activity = 50 Bq; 1 mark: correct fraction remaining used; 1 mark: short half-life reduces radiation dose after scan; 1 mark: must be long enough to complete the scan — trade-off identified; 1 mark: gamma emitter preferred / alpha would be most dangerous internally]

knowledge_checks.q: What experimental evidence led to the replacement of the plum pudding model of the atom?
options: Electrons were discovered orbiting the nucleus at fixed distances
Alpha particles fired at gold foil mostly passed through, but some bounced back
X-ray images showed the nucleus is dense and positive
Neutrons were found to have no charge inside the nucleus

knowledge_checks.q: Which type of radiation is stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium?
The half-life of a radioactive isotope is the time taken for its activity to fall to _____ of its original value.
In alpha decay, the mass number of the nucleus decreases by _____ and the atomic number decreases by 2.
Match each atomic model to the scientist who proposed it:
right: Dalton — atoms as tiny indivisible balls
Thomson — positive sphere with embedded electrons
Rutherford — tiny dense positive nucleus, mostly empty space

flashcard_questions.q: What is the plum pudding model of the atom?
flashcard_questions.a: Thomson's model: a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded throughout, like plums in a pudding.

flashcard_questions.q: What experiment provided evidence for the nuclear model of the atom?
flashcard_questions.a: The Rutherford-Geiger-Marsden alpha particle scattering experiment using thin gold foil (results published 1911).
Atoms of the same element with the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons.

flashcard_questions.q: What does an alpha particle consist of?
flashcard_questions.a: Two protons and two neutrons (a helium-4 nucleus).

flashcard_questions.q: How does alpha emission affect the nucleus?
flashcard_questions.a: Mass number decreases by 4; atomic number decreases by 2.

flashcard_questions.q: How does beta emission affect the nucleus?
flashcard_questions.a: Atomic number increases by 1; mass number is unchanged (a neutron converts to a proton).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the half-life of a radioactive isotope?
flashcard_questions.a: The time for the activity (or number of undecayed nuclei) to fall to half its original value.

flashcard_questions.q: After 3 half-lives, what fraction of the original radioactive nuclei remain?
What is the difference between contamination and irradiation?
flashcard_questions.a: Contamination is radioactive material on or inside the body (ongoing risk); irradiation is external exposure (stops when source moves away).

flashcard_questions.q: Why are alpha sources particularly dangerous if contamination occurs inside the body?
flashcard_questions.a: Alpha particles are strongly ionising and cause significant cell damage, but are stopped before reaching the body from outside.

flashcard_questions.q: Who discovered the neutron and when?

glossary_terms.definition: An early model of the atom as a tiny, solid, indivisible sphere — the starting point of atomic theory in the 19th century.
Thomson's model of the atom as a sphere of positive charge with negative electrons embedded throughout, like plums in a Christmas pudding.
The model in which an atom has a tiny, dense, positively charged nucleus at its centre, with electrons orbiting at much larger distances — almost all of the atom is empty space.
A subatomic particle found in the nucleus that has no electrical charge and a relative mass of 1.
Atoms of the same element that have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons — and therefore different mass numbers.
An unstable nucleus that spontaneously emits radiation in order to reach a more stable state.

Alpha particles (helium nuclei) are the most ionising but least penetrating radiation; beta particles (electrons) are moderately ionising; gamma rays (electromagnetic waves) are the least ionising but most penetrating.
The time taken for the number of radioactive nuclei in a sample — or its activity — to fall to half the original value.
The unwanted deposit of radioactive material on or inside the body, which continues to emit radiation even after the source is removed from proximity.
Exposure to radiation from an external source; once the source is removed, exposure ceases.
